title: [The chief lakes of China Proper]
caption_extra: Lakes. "The chief lakes of China Proper are:—"

rows: The Tungting lake in Hunan. In summer, when it receives the overflow of the Yangtze, its dimensions reach 75 miles in length and 56 in breadth (2000 sq. miles); but in winter the lake empties its waters into the Yangtze and becomes merely an enormous marsh, with two main river channels passing through it, the Yuenkiang and Siangkiang. In 1910 the provincial authorities made a start of dredging the lake, a machine having been bought for that purpose in Germany. title: [Mongols outside Mongolia]
caption_extra: Mongols Outside Mongolia. The greater part of these are the remains of the once powerful Oleut (Oirat) confederation who struggled for a century with the Manchus for the Chinese throne. They consist of:

rows: The hoshun of the Alashan Oleuts (west of the bend of the Yellow River) under a prince of the first class, claiming descent from the brother of Genghiz Khan, and the hoshun of the Etsin-gol Torguts (on the river of the same name in Central Asia);—the first are supervised by the Ning-hsia Tu-tung,—the second, by the authorities of Chinese Turkestan;
The 29 hoshuns of Kokonor and Tsaidam Mongols, supervised by the Chinese resident at Hsi-ning; Kokonor, or Ch'ing-hai, was made a Chinese province in 1911;
The Mongols of Ili and Tarbagatai (ancient Dzungaria), supervised by the Chinese authorities of Sinkiang (Chinese Turkestan)—namely;
four hoshuns of Harashar Torguts on the Yulduz river;
two hoshuns of Kurkarausu Torguts on the Djirgalan river;
one hoshun of Chingho Torguts on the Chingho river;
three hoshuns of Tarbagatai Torguts near Kobur-sar, and a group of Torguts, without princes, on the Tekes and Kungues rivers;
three hoshuns of Hoshuts on the Yulduz river;
a group of Chahars in the Borotala valley;

two groups of Oleuts on the Tekes and Kash rivers. Neither the Chahars, nor the Oleuts have princes, and some small groups of them are moreover to be found in Tarbagatai. Most of the Ili and Tarbagatai Mongols are the Kalmucks which returned here from the Volga valley in 1771;

The Mongols of the Altai district, consisting of two hoshuns of Torguts on the rivers Bulugun and Chingli, one hoshun of Hoshuts, seven hoshuns of Altai Urianghais, some Kirghiz and the former military colonies near Bulun-tohoi; most of these Mongols also returned from the Volga; up to 1907 the Altai district was part of the Kobdo governorship of Outer Mongolia; it was then made into an independent administration unit under a governor at Shara-sume (Ch'enghwasze) and has lately been included in the dominions of the Sinkiang Tu-chün;

A group of Darhats, formerly belonging to the Urga Living Buddha, in the Urianghai territory, which lies between the Sayan and the Tannu-Ula mountain ranges in the north-western extremity of Outer Mongolia. The majority of the Tannu-Urianghai population, excepting the Darhats, are of Turkish origin and speak a Turkish dialect. Their several hoshuns were ruled by hereditary or elective princes.

The Mannai-Oleut hoshun west of Tsitsihar in Manchuria—a group of Oleuts deported here by the Manchus after the destruction of their federation in 1758 and now ruled by a hereditary prince under the supervision of the authorities of the Heilungkiang province;

The Mongol bannermen, belonging to the eight Mongol banners of the Manchu dynasty's bodyguards, who are to be found in the various localities in which the Manchu bannermen were distributed, but chiefly in and near Peking; they are administered by officers appointed by the Central Government, are very poor and play no rôle in any respect.

title: [Gold coins issued within the domain of China in modern times]
caption_extra: Gold. Modern times have witnessed the issue of the following gold coins within the domain of China:

rows: T'aiping tael coin, issued at Nanking during the T'aiping rebellion (1850-1864). The denomination was not embossed on the coin, which was meant to represent 25 taels in silver.
The first gold coin, called tilla, was introduced in Chinese Turkestan during Yakub Beg's rule there,—1870-1877. It bore Mohammedan inscriptions and the portrait of the Sultan of Turkey.
Another issue of gold coins in Turkestan dates back to the rule of Kwang Hsu (1889-1908), the denominations being 1 and 2 mace.
A gold coin was issued in Tibet in 1910.

In 1919 two gold coins, in denominations of $10 and $20, fineness 0.850, bearing the effigy of Yuan Shih-kai, were minted in Tientsin. They were intended to serve currency purposes, but with the collapse of Yuan Shih-kai's ambitious scheme to become Emperor the plan to circulate the gold coins was abandoned.

Due to the World War silver supplies ceased to reach the far-off province of Yunnan. Therefore the then governor, T'ang Chi-yao, issued, towards the close of 1919, about 900,000 gold coins of a denomination of 10 dollars each. A second gold coin, inscribed 5 dollars, followed shortly thereafter, both bearing the portrait of T'ang. With the fall in the price of silver holders of those gold coins promptly sold them. These coins were melted down and the gold exported again.
